summary: Describes how to carry audio from the MELPe speech codec in RTP packets. It supports the codec's three encoding rates and frame sizes, and spells out comfort noise and packet loss concealment.

eli5.summary: A talking-robot code squeezes speech into tiny bits. This says how to pack those bits into mail envelopes so the other end can play them back, even if one gets lost.

subtitle: How to carry the NATO-standard MELPe low-bitrate speech codec inside RTP packets, at 2400, 1200 or 600 bps.

tldr.problem: MELPe is a very low-bitrate speech codec used in military and government communications, and VoIP systems need to carry it without decoding and re-encoding it, which would hurt intelligibility.
tldr.mechanism: Each MELPe frame is packed into whole octets (7, 11 or 7 octets for the 2400, 1200 and 600 bps rates) and sent as the RTP payload, with no extra payload header. Reserved bits in each frame identify the bitrate, and special rules cover comfort noise and packet loss concealment.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can negotiate the bitrate in SDP, send one or more frames per packet, and switch rates dynamically when both sides support it.

today: RFC 8130 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the RTP payload definition for MELPe.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8130 describes how speech compressed by the Mixed Excitation Linear Prediction Enhanced (MELPe) codec is formatted as an RTP payload. It covers the three codec bitrates (2400, 1200 and 600 bps) and how to put their data frames into RTP packets.

A sender may put one or more codec frames in each packet, depending on the application, network conditions, bandwidth limits, delay requirements and tolerance for packet loss.
sections.eli5: MELPe is a way of shrinking a voice into very few bits. This document is the packing list for putting those bits into internet packets.

sections.title: The MELPe Codec
sections.content:
MELP was developed by the US military as an upgrade from the LPC-based CELP standard vocoder for low-bitrate communications. It was further enhanced and adopted by NATO as MELPe for military and other governmental communications, under the name STANAG 4591. Commercial and civilian uses have since arisen because of its low bitrate and relatively high intelligibility.

VoIP and SIP systems need to transport MELPe without decoding and re-encoding it, to preserve intelligibility. That is why a payload format is needed.

The basic 2400 bps coder uses a 22.5 ms frame of 180 samples (8000 Hz, 16 bits each). The 1200 and 600 bps coders use three and four 22.5 ms frames respectively. Payload sizes are 54, 81 and 54 bits for the 2400, 1200 and 600 bps frames. Dynamic bitrate switching is permitted, but only if both endpoints support it.

The coder treats voiced and unvoiced speech differently. Forward error correction (FEC) is applied to unvoiced speech at 2400 bps only; the lower-rate coders rely on error protection in the channel.
sections.eli5: The codec chops speech into tiny slices and describes each slice with very few numbers. A slow setting uses fewer numbers per second but sounds less clear.

sections.title: The Payload and Bitstream Layout
sections.content:
The RTP payload is simply one or more MELPe frames. No payload-specific header is needed. Because the codec uses 22.5, 67.5 or 90 ms frames at an 8 kHz clock, the RTP timestamp MUST be in units of 1/8000 of a second. When a packet holds several frames, the timestamp is that of the oldest frame. The RTP payload type is not assigned here; a profile may assign one, or a dynamic one is chosen by the sender.

A 2400 bps frame uses 54 bits, which fit in 7 octets with two unused bits. A 1200 bps frame uses 81 bits in 11 octets (seven unused bits). A 600 bps frame uses 54 bits in 7 octets. Bit B_01 goes in the least significant bit of the first octet and the rest follow in order. The unused bits, named RSVA, RSVB and RSVC, carry the bitrate indicator described below.

The RFC gives the bit-by-bit meaning of each bit position for all three rates (gain, pitch and voicing, line spectral frequencies, Fourier magnitudes and so on), taken from the NATO specification. In the original bitstream the most significant bits were priority bits meant for stronger channel protection; that is irrelevant on IP, but the bitstreams are presented identically so gateways stay interoperable.
sections.eli5: Each slice of speech becomes a tiny parcel of 54 or 81 bits, padded out to whole bytes. The parcels are always packed in the same order so everyone can unpack them.

sections.title: Several Frames per Packet
sections.content:
A packet may hold zero or more coder frames followed by zero or one comfort noise frame. The default packetization interval is one coder frame (22.5, 67.5 or 90 ms depending on the rate); a longer interval reduces the packet rate. A packet with no frames at all MAY be sent periodically to show connectivity to an otherwise idle receiver.

All frames in one packet MUST be the same bitrate, and frames MUST NOT be split between packets. The number of frames is not sent: the receiver counts the payload octets and divides by the expected size per frame (7, 11 or 7 octets). The last frame can be a 2-octet comfort noise frame. Fewer frames per packet means lower delay; more frames suit bandwidth-limited or delay-insensitive uses.

When bitrate switching is used, the reserved bits tell the receiver which kind of frame it has (see the table). If switching is not used, reserved bits are sent as 0 and ignored. When a packet has several frames, it is RECOMMENDED to inspect the last octet, and if that indicates comfort noise, the third last octet.

On congestion, the target bitrate can be changed at any time, and the amount of speech per packet can be changed too. Applications running RTP over UDP SHOULD add their own congestion control and MAY use a transport circuit breaker.
sections.eli5: You can put one parcel or several in an envelope, but never cut a parcel in half. Sending fewer parcels per envelope is faster but uses more envelopes.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP
sections.content:
The format is registered as the audio subtypes MELP, MELP2400, MELP1200 and MELP600. The names with a rate in them were used by early implementations and are kept; they fix the rate and MUST NOT carry a bitrate parameter. Optional parameters are ptime, maxptime and bitrate, a comma-separated list chosen from 2400, 1200 and 600 in order of preference. If bitrate is absent, the fixed rate of 2400 MUST be used.

In SDP, the encoding name SHALL be MELP, and bitrate goes in the a=fmtp line. The ptime value cannot select the mode, because some values are ambiguous: ptime=68 could mean one 67.5 ms frame or three 22.5 ms frames.

In offer/answer, bitrate is bidirectional. Both sides MUST use a common value, the offer lists the offerer's rates in preference order, and the initial rate is the first one in the answer. With an offer of 2400,600 and an answer of 600,2400, the initial bitrate is 600. A lower rate matters when an endpoint is on a bandwidth-constrained link, such as a 1200 bps radio link or slower.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two sides swap a list of speeds they can handle and agree on one, like picking a walking speed you can both keep up.

sections.title: Comfort Noise, Silence and Packet Loss
sections.content:
MELPe is mainly used for radio voice, where transmissions normally stop and start. Gaps in RTP sequence numbers mean lost packets, which are filled by packet loss concealment (PLC), while an abrupt end of packets means an intended pause. A coder may send a comfort noise frame before it stops, and a receiver may play comfort noise during silence. No SDP negotiation is needed.

Comfort noise follows Appendix B of SCIP-210. Only two parameters are carried (the first line spectral frequency set and the second gain), in a 13-bit frame sent in 2 octets. After voice activity detection stops indicating speech, at least two comfort noise frames are transmitted as a grace period.

PLC uses the pitch/voicing parameter of the 2400 bps coder. A value of zero means non-voiced, and valid pitch values have at least three bits set, so a value with exactly two bits set can signal an erasure. The preferred erasure code is 3: bits P0 and P1 set to one and P2 to P6 set to zero. In 1200 and 600 bps modes, the 2400 bps decoder is called three or four times to cover one lost frame.
sections.eli5: When nobody is talking, the codec can send a tiny note saying 'it is quiet here'. If a packet goes missing, a special marker tells the player to fill the hole instead of playing garbage.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets using this format are subject to the security considerations of RTP and any applicable profile (RTP/AVP, RTP/AVPF, RTP/SAVP, RTP/SAVPF). The RFC notes that securing RTP is the responsibility of whoever uses RTP in an application, and that applications SHOULD use one or more appropriate strong security mechanisms.

Specific to the payload format: neither it nor the MELPe decoder shows significant non-uniformity in receiver-side computational complexity, so pathological data is unlikely to cause denial of service, and the format has no active content. The RFC also points to RFC 6562 on voice activity detection and its effect on bitrates.
sections.eli5: The envelopes themselves are boring and safe to open. If you want them sealed and signed, use the usual RTP security tools.
